title: SE201 Lesson 6: Quality, feedback, and observability

scenes.text: Software engineering two oh one. Lesson six. [pause] Quality, feedback, and observability.

data.headline:
Quality, feedback,
and observability.
data.sub: From loop to enterprise systems  •  clarkhuang.github.io

scenes.text: Picture a made-up billing system. Last night, it renewed its subscriptions. This morning the build is green, and every test passed. Was every customer charged the right amount, exactly once? [pause] Yes, the tests passed? Probably, coverage is high? Or: you can't tell from that? [pause] <emphasis>You can't tell from that.</emphasis> Green says the code did what its tests asked. It says nothing about what happened last night.

data.question:
The build is green. Every test passed. Was every
customer charged the right amount, exactly once?
data.why:
Green is about
the code. Not
about last night.

scenes.text: Back to the lens from lesson one: architecture bends around what's scarce. Ten years ago, the scarce thing was seeing the whole system. The answer was observability: logs, metrics, traces. They answer: what happened?

data.label: THE LENS FROM LESSON ONE  ·  ARCHITECTURE BENDS AROUND WHAT’S SCARCE

scenes.text: Now the scarce thing is knowing it's right. That's a different question. And no dashboard can answer it, until somebody has written down what right means. [pause] So: define right, up front. Watch every run. And feed back what you learn.

data.label: THE LENS FROM LESSON ONE  ·  ARCHITECTURE BENDS AROUND WHAT’S SCARCE

scenes.text: Take our made-up example: the subscription-billing system from lesson one. Here are last night's renewals. And the build is green. [pause] But no test ever looked at this table. So was last night right? The green can't say.

data.label: A MADE-UP EXAMPLE  ·  THE BILLING SYSTEM, THE MORNING AFTER

checks.text:
Each charge equals
the plan’s price

scenes.text: So before the work starts, write down what right means, in the business's words. Every renewal charged the right amount, exactly once. Then split that into checks an agent can run. One: none was charged twice. Two: each charge equals the plan's price. Three: every renewal that was due was attempted.

data.label: A MADE-UP EXAMPLE  ·  THE BILLING SYSTEM, THE MORNING AFTER

checks.text:
Each charge equals
the plan’s price

data.caption: Right: every renewal charged the right amount, exactly once.

scenes.text: Now run them, on last night's real renewals. [pause] One was charged twice. One, the wrong amount. One was never attempted. [pause] And look at the totals: they match. Three wrong renewals, inside a sum that's exactly right. So check every renewal, not just the total.

data.label: A MADE-UP EXAMPLE  ·  THE BILLING SYSTEM, THE MORNING AFTER

checks.text:
Each charge equals
the plan’s price

data.caption: Check every renewal, not just the total.

scenes.text: That one sentence does double duty. You write the check once, and run it twice. Before a change ships, on sample renewals, in the pipeline. And after every nightly run, on the real ones. [pause] Add a target for time, too. A service level objective, an S.L.O.: say, ninety-nine point nine percent of renewals due today, attempted by six A.M. Now an agent can run all of it, without asking anyone what good looks like.

data.label: WRITE THE CHECK ONCE  ·  RUN IT TWICE

scenes.text: The checks say that something is wrong. The record says why. So every step of every run leaves a line, in a shape that people and agents can both read. Here's the double charge. Attempt one: a timeout. Attempt two, with a new key: charged. Then reconcile, against the processor's own report: two charges. The first attempt had gone through. [pause] Nobody has to guess.

data.label: WATCH EVERY RUN  ·  EVERY STEP LEAVES A RECORD  ·  A MADE-UP EXAMPLE

bands.label: THE RECORD FOR RENEWAL R-1043, STEP BY STEP

nodes.tag: ONE LINE PER STEP  ·  PEOPLE AND AGENTS CAN BOTH READ IT

data.caption: A timeout, then a retry with a new key. The first attempt had gone through.
data.foot: THE CHECKS SAY SOMETHING IS WRONG  ·  THE RECORD SAYS WHY

scenes.text: First, put last night right, with a person approving, as in lesson five. Then close the loop. Every miss goes back into the brief, and the checks. The double charge becomes a new line in the brief: a retry must reuse the same key. That's an idempotency key; more in lesson eight. And a new test: the processor times out. [pause] So each run makes the next one better.

data.label: FEED IT BACK  ·  EACH RUN IMPROVES THE NEXT

scenes.text: And be honest about the limit. A check only catches what somebody thought to ask. So a person still reads a sample of real invoices. And whatever they find becomes the next check.

scenes.text: So, to recap. Green doesn't mean right. Define right first, in the business's words. Check before you ship, and after every run. Make every step leave a record. And feed every miss back in.

data.headline: Green doesn’t mean right
items: Define right first, in the business’s words
Check before you ship, and after every run

scenes.text: Which gives us rule six, for your agents. Before you build, write down what right means, as checks you can run, in the business's words. Run them before a change ships, and after every run. Leave a record at every step. When a check fails, stop and tell a person. And feed every miss back into the brief and the checks.

Run them before a change ships, and after every run.
Leave a record at every step.
When a check fails, stop and tell a person.
Feed every miss back into the brief and the checks.

scenes.text: Now, your turn. Pick one job your system runs every day. Ask your A.I.: what would have to be true for last night's run to be right? Write it as three read-only checks I can run on the real data. [pause] Then run one.

scenes.text: Once a job has a brief, its checks, and a record of every run, it's ready to be reused. That's next: skills as building blocks. See you in lesson seven.
